title: Functions and references
bridge: C++ functions declare a return type and parameter types: `int clampValue(int v, int lo, int hi)`. Parameters are **copies** by default; add `&` (`int& health`) to let the function change the caller's variable. Functions must be declared above where they're used (or announced with a prototype).
lesson:
```
int clampValue(int v, int lo, int hi)
{
    if (v < lo) return lo;
    if (v > hi) return hi;
    return v;
}
```

**Copies vs references.** Normally a function gets a *copy*:

```
void hit(int health) { health -= 10; }   // changes the copy only
int h = 50; hit(h);                       // h is still 50!
```

Put `&` after the type and the parameter becomes another name for the caller's variable:

```
void hit(int& health) { health -= 10; }
int h = 50; hit(h);                       // h is now 40
```

That's how C++ functions "give back" more than one result, and why game code is full of `&`. `void` means the function returns nothing.

**Order matters.** C++ reads top to bottom, so a function must appear before it's called. In bigger programs you put declarations (prototypes) in a `.h` header file and the code in a `.cpp` file. Unreal does exactly this: `Turret.h` and `Turret.cpp`.

You can also give a parameter a default: `void heal(int& h, int amount = 10)`.

exercises.title: Take damage
exercises.prompt: Fix void addDamage so it really lowers the caller's health by dmg, never going below 0.

tests.hint_if_fail: The function changes a copy. Make health a reference: int& health.

tests.why: Use a reference parameter: int& health

hints: Without & the function gets its own copy.
void addDamage(int& health, int dmg) { health -= dmg; if (health < 0) health = 0; }

exercises.title: Swap
exercises.prompt: Write void swapValues(int& a, int& b) that swaps the two variables.

tests.call: []{ int a = 1, b = 2; swapValues(a, b); return a * 10 + b; }()
[]{ int a = 7, b = 7; swapValues(a, b); return a * 10 + b; }()

tests.why: Write it yourself this time, without std::swap.

hints: You need a third variable to hold one value for a moment.
int t = a; a = b; b = t;
